overview.title: Compile, preprocess, fit and predict on MNIST
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.1 A first look at a neural network
overview.main_topic: Finishing the compile call (loss and metrics), reshaping and rescaling the MNIST images, training with `fit()` for 5 epochs in batches of 128, and reading the probability vector returned by `predict()`.
overview.central_idea: Training a Keras model is a short pipeline: compile with loss/metrics, turn the raw `uint8` images into flat `float32` vectors in [0, 1], call `fit()`, then call `predict()` and interpret the 10 softmax probabilities per image.
overview.importance: These four listings are the canonical Keras workflow that the entire book reuses (compile, preprocess, fit, predict). The page also shows concretely what the softmax output looks like and how to read a prediction, and introduces epochs and batch size, which section 2.4 and 2.5 will explain.
learning_objectives: State why the images are reshaped from (60000, 28, 28) to (60000, 784) and rescaled from [0, 255] to [0, 1].
Explain the roles of `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` and `metrics=["accuracy"]` in `compile()`.
Read `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128)` and say what an epoch and a batch are.
Interpret the 10-element array returned by `model.predict()` for a single digit and identify the predicted class.
prerequisites: The two-layer Dense/softmax model and the three compile ingredients from p.43.
The MNIST arrays and their shapes from p.42.

summary:
The page opens with the tail of **Listing 2.3**: `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` and `metrics=["accuracy"]`, completing the compile call started on p.43 (the optimizer was `"adam"`).

Next comes **preprocessing**. The training images were stored as a `uint8` array of shape `(60000, 28, 28)` with values in `[0, 255]`. **Listing 2.4** reshapes them to `(60000, 28 * 28)`, i.e. one flat 784-vector per image, converts to `float32`, and divides by 255 so all values lie in `[0, 1]`. The same is done for the 10,000 test images. This gives the model the shape it expects and a well-scaled input range.

**Listing 2.5** trains the model with a single call: `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128)`. The authors describe this as *fitting* the model to its training data. During training two quantities are displayed: the loss over the training data and the accuracy over the training data; the model quickly reaches 0.989 (98.9 %) training accuracy.

With a trained model, **Listing 2.6** predicts class probabilities for *new* digits: `test_digits = test_images[0:10]`, `predictions = model.predict(test_digits)`. `predictions[0]` is a 10-element `float32` array; entry `i` is the probability that `test_digits[0]` belongs to class `i`. The largest entry, 9.9999106e-01 (almost 1), is at index 7, so the model says the first test digit is a 7. The page ends mid-sentence; p.45 checks this against the test label and evaluates on the full test set.

paragraphs.excerpt: Before training, we'll preprocess the data by reshaping it into the shape
paragraphs.what_it_says: Before training, the data is preprocessed in two ways: reshaped into the shape the model expects, and scaled so all values are in [0, 1]. The training images were a `uint8` array of shape `(60000, 28, 28)` with values in [0, 255]; they become a `float32` array of shape `(60000, 28 * 28)` with values between 0 and 1.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The Dense layers of p.43 consume one vector per sample, so each 28x28 grid must be flattened to a 784-vector. Dividing by 255 moves pixel intensities from byte range to the unit interval, and `float32` is the numeric type the network's weights and arithmetic use.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Two universal habits in deep learning appear here: match the tensor shape to the model's input and feed small, floating-point values. Chapter 2.2 (p.45 onward) formalizes shapes, axes and dtypes; chapter 4 does similar preprocessing for text (p.139) and tabular data (p.152).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Shape change `(60000, 28, 28) -> (60000, 784)` keeps the number of elements (60000 x 784 = 47,040,000) and only reinterprets the layout; the division is element-wise and broadcasts the scalar 255 over the whole array.

terminology.meaning: Transform raw data into the form (shape, type, range) the model expects before training.
Unsigned 8-bit integer type, values 0 to 255; the natural storage type for grayscale pixels.
32-bit floating-point type, the standard numeric type for neural-network computation.

connections: p.42: the original arrays and their shapes.
p.75: section 2.5 restates that the inputs are float32 tensors of shape (60000, 784) and (10000, 784).
p.58: tensor reshaping is explained in section 2.3.4.

paragraphs.excerpt: We're now ready to train the model, which in Keras is done via
paragraphs.what_it_says: Training in Keras is done by calling the model's `fit()` method: we fit the model to its training data. Listing 2.5 follows.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Fit' is the statistics word for adjusting a model's parameters so that it matches data. One method call hides the whole loop of batching, forward pass, loss, gradient and weight update.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: `fit()` is the workhorse of the book; p.76 explains what it does internally, and section 2.5.3 (p.81) reimplements the loop by hand.

terminology.meaning: Adjust the model's weights to the training data; in Keras, the `model.fit()` method.

connections: p.76: what happens when you call `fit`: mini-batches of 128, 5 times over, gradient updates via backpropagation.

paragraphs.excerpt: Two quantities are displayed during training: the loss of the model over
paragraphs.what_it_says: During training, two quantities are displayed: the loss over the training data and the accuracy over the training data. The model quickly reaches 0.989 (98.9 %) accuracy on the training data.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These are precisely the loss and metric chosen at compile time. The number 0.989 is a *training* accuracy; p.45 reveals the test accuracy is lower (97.8 %), which the authors use to introduce overfitting.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Learning to read the training log (loss should go down, accuracy up) is the first diagnostic skill of the practitioner, and the distinction between training and test accuracy is the first lesson in generalization.

terminology.meaning: Fraction of training samples classified correctly, measured on the data the model learns from.

connections: p.43: loss and metrics were defined as compile ingredients.
p.45: test accuracy 97.8 % vs 98.9 % training accuracy, an example of overfitting.

paragraphs.excerpt: Now that we have a trained model, we can use it to predict class
paragraphs.what_it_says: With a trained model we can predict class probabilities for *new* digits, i.e. images that were not part of the training data, such as those in the test set.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The emphasis on *new* is the point of the whole exercise: a model is only useful if it works on inputs it has never seen. The test set was held out precisely to play this role.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the inference phase of the workflow stated on p.43: produce predictions for `test_images` and compare them with `test_labels`.

terminology.meaning: Using a trained model to produce outputs for new inputs (here via `predict()`).

connections: p.43: the workflow announced that predictions would be made on `test_images`.

paragraphs.excerpt: Each number of index i in that array corresponds to the probability that
paragraphs.what_it_says: Each number at index `i` in the printed array is the probability that `test_digits[0]` belongs to class `i`. The first test digit has its highest score, 0.99999106 (almost 1), at index 7, so the model says it is a 7.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The output of the softmax layer from p.43 is being read: the position of the largest probability is the predicted class, and because the classes are the digits 0-9, index 7 means 'the digit 7'. The other nine entries are tiny (1e-6 to 1e-14) and together make up the remaining 0.00001.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the concrete meaning of a classifier's output and of the `argmax` rule used on p.45 to turn probabilities into a label.
paragraphs.technical_idea: For a softmax output `p`, the predicted class is `argmax_i p[i]`; here `p[7] = 9.9999106e-01` dominates.

terminology.meaning: The model's estimated probability that an input belongs to a given class; the ten of them sum to 1.

connections: p.43: the 10-way softmax layer returns 10 probability scores summing to 1.
p.45: `predictions[0].argmax()` gives 7 and is compared with `test_labels[0]`.

concepts.name: Preprocessing (reshape and rescale)
concepts.definition: Transforming raw input data into the shape, dtype and value range the model expects before training.
concepts.intuition: Flatten each picture into one long list of numbers and shrink the numbers from 0-255 to 0-1 so the network starts from well-behaved inputs.
concepts.technical: `reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` turns each 28x28 grid into a 784-vector; `astype("float32") / 255` converts to floating point and scales into [0, 1].
concepts.significance: Dense layers require vector inputs, and gradient-based training behaves much better with small, similarly scaled inputs; the same two steps appear in every example of the book.
concepts.example: Listing 2.4 applies the same operations to the 60,000 training and 10,000 test images.
concepts.misconception: Reshaping does not change or reorder pixel values; it only changes how the same elements are indexed.

concepts.name: Sparse categorical cross-entropy loss
concepts.definition: The loss used for multiclass classification with integer labels; it measures how far the predicted probability distribution is from the true class.
concepts.intuition: Penalize the model by how little probability it gave to the correct digit.
concepts.technical: For a sample with true class `y` and predicted probabilities `p`, the loss is `-log p[y]`. 'Sparse' means the labels are integers (0-9) rather than one-hot vectors.
concepts.significance: Pairs naturally with a softmax output; it is the standard loss for classification throughout the book (see p.143 for the categorical variant).
concepts.example: If the model assigns probability 0.99999106 to the true class 7, the loss is -log(0.99999106) ≈ 8.9e-6, nearly zero.
concepts.misconception: 'Sparse' refers to the label format, not to the model or to sparsity of weights.

concepts.name: Epoch and batch size
concepts.definition: An epoch is one full pass over the training data; the batch size is the number of samples processed per weight update.
concepts.intuition: Read the whole textbook five times (epochs), studying 128 pages at a time (batches) and adjusting your understanding after each chunk.
concepts.technical: With 60,000 samples and `batch_size=128`, each epoch has ceil(60000 / 128) = 469 updates, so 5 epochs perform 2,345 gradient updates (p.76).
concepts.significance: These two hyperparameters control how long training runs and how noisy each update is; they are explained in section 2.4.3 (mini-batch SGD, p.67).
concepts.misconception: One epoch is not one weight update; it is hundreds of updates, one per batch.

concepts.name: fit()
concepts.definition: The Keras method that trains a compiled model on training data and targets.
concepts.intuition: Press 'learn': the model iterates over the data, measuring the loss and updating its weights, printing loss and metrics as it goes.
concepts.technical: Iterates `epochs` times over the data in mini-batches of `batch_size`; for each batch computes the loss gradient with backpropagation and moves the weights (p.76).
concepts.significance: It is the single call that performs learning in the standard workflow compile -> fit -> evaluate/predict (p.230).
concepts.example: Listing 2.5 reaches 98.9 % training accuracy in 5 epochs.
concepts.misconception: `fit()` does not evaluate generalization by itself; without validation data, the printed accuracy is on training data only.

concepts.name: predict() and reading softmax outputs
concepts.definition: The Keras method that returns the model's outputs for a batch of new inputs; for this model, a (n, 10) array of class probabilities.
concepts.intuition: Ask the trained model 'what is this?' and get ten probabilities, one per digit, that add up to one.
concepts.technical: `model.predict(test_digits)` with `test_digits` of shape (10, 784) returns shape (10, 10). The predicted class is the index of the maximum entry.
concepts.significance: This is inference, the reason the model was trained; its output format follows directly from the softmax layer on p.43.
concepts.example: `predictions[0]` has 9.9999106e-01 at index 7, so the first test digit is predicted to be a 7.
concepts.misconception: `predict()` returns probabilities, not labels; a separate `argmax` (p.45) is needed to obtain the digit.

math.title: Rescaling pixel values to [0, 1]

variables.meaning: A pixel intensity stored as uint8 (0 = black, 255 = white).
The same intensity as a float32 in the unit interval.

math.operations: Element-wise division of every entry of the array by the scalar 255 (the scalar is broadcast over the whole tensor).
math.purpose: Put all inputs on a small, common scale that gradient-based training handles well.
math.interpretation: The image content is unchanged; only the units change, from 'byte values' to 'fraction of full brightness'.
math.intuition: Weights initialized to small random values produce reasonable outputs for inputs around 0-1, but would produce huge activations for inputs up to 255.
math.numerical_example: A mid-gray pixel 128 becomes 128/255 ≈ 0.502; black 0 stays 0; white 255 becomes 1.0.

math.title: Reshaping keeps the element count

variables.meaning: Number of training images (the samples axis, unchanged).
Height and width of one image, merged into a single axis of 784 features.

math.operations: Merge the last two axes into one; no values are created, removed or modified.
math.purpose: Give each image the flat vector form that the Dense layers of Listing 2.2 expect.
math.interpretation: The sample axis is preserved so the model still sees 60,000 independent examples, each described by 784 numbers.
math.intuition: Read the 28 rows of a picture one after the other to make one long row.
math.numerical_example: Pixel at (row r, column c) of an image lands at flat index 28*r + c; e.g. (3, 5) -> 89.

math.title: Number of gradient updates in 5 epochs
math.source_text: model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128) (the counts 469 and 2,345 are stated on p.76)

variables.meaning: `epochs`: number of passes over the training set.

math.operations: Integer division rounded up (the last batch of an epoch has only 60000 - 468*128 = 96 samples), then multiplication by the number of epochs.
math.purpose: Connect the two `fit()` arguments to the amount of learning actually performed.
math.interpretation: Each update moves all 407,050 weights a little in the direction that lowers the loss on the current batch of 128 images.
math.intuition: Small batches mean many cheap, slightly noisy updates per epoch rather than one expensive exact one.

math.title: Reading the prediction: argmax of the probability vector
math.source_text: "This first test digit has the highest probability score (0.99999106, almost 1) at index 7, so according to our model, it must be a 7"

variables.meaning: Entry i of `predictions[0]`: the probability that `test_digits[0]` is digit i.
The predicted digit, the index of the largest probability.

math.operations: Find the index of the maximum of the 10 probabilities.
math.purpose: Turn the softmax distribution into a single class decision.
math.interpretation: p_7 = 9.9999106e-01; all the other entries together are about 8.9e-6, so the decision is essentially certain for this sample.
math.intuition: The model's bet is the digit it gives the most probability to.
math.numerical_example: From the printed array: p_3 = 8.4e-06 is the runner-up, more than 100,000 times smaller than p_7.

code.what_it_does: Completes `model.compile(optimizer="adam", ...)` by naming the loss function and the list of metrics to monitor.

line_explanations.explanation: `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"`: the loss for multiclass classification when labels are integers (0-9) and the model outputs softmax probabilities; it is -log of the probability assigned to the true class.
`metrics=["accuracy"]`: report the fraction of correctly classified samples during training and evaluation.
Closes the compile call; the model is now configured but still untrained.

code.inputs_outputs: Configuration only; no data flows and nothing is returned.
code.algorithm: Records the optimizer, loss and metric objects that `fit()` and `evaluate()` will use.
code.theory_link: The loss is the 'how the model measures its performance' ingredient and the metric the 'what to monitor' ingredient defined on p.43.

parameters.name: loss
parameters.role: Scalar objective minimized by the optimizer.

parameters.name: metrics
parameters.role: Values displayed and returned but not optimized.

pitfalls: Use `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` with integer labels; with one-hot labels you need `categorical_crossentropy` instead (p.143 discusses the alternative).

code.title: Preparing the image data
code.original_code:
train_images = train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))
train_images = train_images.astype("float32") / 255
test_images = test_images.reshape((10000, 28 * 28))
test_images = test_images.astype("float32") / 255
code.what_it_does: Flattens each 28x28 image into a 784-element vector and rescales pixel values from integers in [0, 255] to float32 values in [0, 1], for both training and test sets.

line_explanations.explanation: Reshape the training array from (60000, 28, 28) to (60000, 784); `28 * 28` is written out to make the origin of 784 visible.
Convert uint8 to float32, then divide by 255 element-wise; the result lies in [0, 1].
Apply exactly the same transformation to the 10,000 test images so that test inputs match what the model was trained on.

code.inputs_outputs: In: `train_images` (60000, 28, 28) uint8, `test_images` (10000, 28, 28) uint8. Out: (60000, 784) and (10000, 784) float32 arrays with values in [0, 1].
code.algorithm: Two NumPy operations per array: a view-level reshape and an element-wise type cast plus division.
code.theory_link: Reshaping is the tensor operation of section 2.3.4 (p.58); the division is an element-wise operation with scalar broadcasting (sections 2.3.1-2.3.2). The result is the (60000, 784) tensor section 2.5 (p.75) refers to.

parameters.role: Target shape: samples axis kept, image axes merged.

parameters.name: "float32"
parameters.role: Target dtype matching the model's weights.
Maximum uint8 pixel value; dividing by it maps the range to [0, 1].

pitfalls: Cast to float *before* dividing; integer division of a uint8 array would produce zeros (or wrong types).
The test set must receive the identical transformation; forgetting it would feed the model values 255 times larger than it saw in training.
Hardcoding 60000 and 10000 works for MNIST; `reshape((-1, 28 * 28))` is the shape-agnostic form.

code.what_it_does: Trains the compiled model on the 60,000 preprocessed images and their labels, making 5 passes over the data in mini-batches of 128 samples, printing loss and accuracy as it goes.

line_explanations.explanation: `train_images` are the inputs, `train_labels` the integer targets; `epochs=5` means five full passes over the data; `batch_size=128` means weights are updated after each group of 128 samples.

code.inputs_outputs: In: (60000, 784) float32 inputs and (60000,) integer labels. Out: a `History` object (not used here) and a printed log of training loss and accuracy per epoch; the model's weights are modified in place.
code.algorithm: For each of 5 epochs, for each of 469 batches: forward pass, sparse categorical cross-entropy loss, gradient via backpropagation, Adam weight update (described on p.76).
code.theory_link: This single call is the gradient-based optimization loop of section 2.4 and is reimplemented by hand in sections 2.5.2-2.5.3 (p.79-81).

parameters.name: epochs
parameters.role: Number of full passes over the training set (5).

parameters.name: batch_size
parameters.role: Samples per gradient update (128), giving 469 updates per epoch.

code.title: Using the model to make predictions
code.what_it_does: Takes the first ten test images, runs them through the trained model, and shows the 10 class probabilities for the first one; index 7 holds 0.99999106, so the prediction is '7'.

line_explanations.explanation: Slice the first 10 preprocessed test images, giving an array of shape (10, 784).
`model.predict` runs the forward pass in inference mode and returns an array of shape (10, 10): one probability vector per image.
The first row. Entries are tiny except index 7 (9.9999106e-01). Index 3 (8.4e-06) is the distant second choice; the dtype is float32.

code.inputs_outputs: In: (10, 784) float32. Out: (10, 10) float32 softmax probabilities; each row sums to 1.
code.algorithm: Forward pass only: `softmax(relu(x · W1 + b1) · W2 + b2)` for each input, no gradient computation.
code.theory_link: Shows the concrete output of the 10-way softmax layer defined on p.43 and the inference step of the workflow announced there.

parameters.name: test_digits
parameters.role: A small batch of unseen inputs.

parameters.name: predictions[0]
parameters.role: Probability vector for the first test digit.

pitfalls: `predict` expects a batch; passing a single 784-vector without a leading axis raises a shape error (use `test_images[0:1]`).
The floating-point values are not exactly summing to 1 in print because of rounding, but they do to float32 precision.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: predicted class and confidence for all ten digits
import numpy as np
print(predictions.shape)              # (10, 10)
print(predictions.argmax(axis=1))     # predicted digit for each of the 10 images
print(predictions.max(axis=1))        # confidence of each prediction
print(predictions[0].sum())           # ~1.0

deeper.title: Why divide by 255 at all?
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: the page says the scaling is done so values are in [0, 1], without saying why that helps. Three reasons, in order of importance:

1. **Initial activations stay sane.** Weights are initialized to small random numbers (roughly ±0.05 for a 784-input layer). With inputs up to 255, the first layer's pre-activations `x · W` would have magnitudes in the hundreds; with inputs in [0, 1] they are of order 1, where relu and softmax behave sensibly.
2. **Gradients stay comparable.** The gradient of the loss with respect to a weight is proportional to the input it multiplies (see section 2.4). Inputs 255 times larger mean gradients 255 times larger, which would require a 255 times smaller learning rate to be stable.
3. **A common scale across features.** All 784 pixels share the same range, so no pixel dominates by virtue of its units. (For tabular data where features have different scales, the book standardizes each feature instead, p.152.)

None of this changes the information in the image; it only makes the optimization problem better conditioned.

deeper.title: What `fit()` is doing while it prints those numbers
deeper.body:
According to p.76, the single call in Listing 2.5 unfolds as follows:

- Split the 60,000 training images into mini-batches of 128 (469 batches per epoch, the last one holding 96 images).
- For each batch: run the forward pass, compute the sparse categorical cross-entropy loss, compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight using backpropagation, and let Adam move the weights a little in the direction that lowers the loss on that batch.
- After each epoch (one full pass), print the average loss and accuracy over the batches seen in that epoch.
- Repeat for 5 epochs: 2,345 updates in total.

The accuracy of 0.989 printed at the end is the running training accuracy of the fifth epoch. Section 2.5.3 (p.81) writes this loop out in plain Python so nothing stays hidden.

deeper.title: Reading the probability array as a bar chart
deeper.body:
Listing 2.6 prints ten numbers in scientific notation. Written as plain decimals the picture is stark:

| class | probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.000 000 000 1 |
| 1 | 0.000 000 000 2 |
| 2 | 0.000 000 06 |
| 3 | 0.000 008 4 |
| 4 | 0.000 000 000 03 |
| 5 | 0.000 000 003 |
| 6 | 0.000 000 000 000 08 |
| 7 | **0.999 991** |
| 8 | 0.000 000 03 |
| 9 | 0.000 000 4 |

The model puts 99.9991 % of its probability mass on '7'. The runner-up is '3' with 0.00084 %, which is plausible: a 7 and a 3 can share a horizontal top stroke. The cross-entropy loss on this sample would be -log(0.99999106) ≈ 0.0000089, essentially zero, which is what a well-trained model should produce on an easy example.

misconceptions.claim: Reshaping the images to 784 vectors loses the spatial information of the picture.
misconceptions.correction: No pixel values are lost; every pixel keeps a fixed position in the vector (index 28*row + col). What the Dense model lacks is any built-in notion of *neighbourhood*; it must learn spatial structure from data. Convnets (chapter 8) are designed to exploit it directly.

misconceptions.claim: 98.9 % accuracy means the model will be right 98.9 % of the time on new digits.
misconceptions.correction: 0.989 is measured on the training data. On the test set the accuracy is 97.8 % (p.45); the gap is overfitting.
It returns a probability vector per input; the digit is obtained by taking the index of the largest probability (`argmax`, p.45).

misconceptions.claim: `epochs=5` means the weights are updated 5 times.
misconceptions.correction: Each epoch contains 469 batches of 128 samples, each producing one update; 5 epochs give 2,345 updates (p.76).

takeaways: `compile()` is completed with `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` (for integer labels and softmax outputs) and `metrics=["accuracy"]`.
Images are reshaped from (60000, 28, 28) uint8 to (60000, 784) float32 and divided by 255 so values lie in [0, 1]; the test set gets the identical treatment.
`model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128)` trains the model; it prints training loss and accuracy and reaches 98.9 % training accuracy.
`model.predict()` returns a 10-probability vector per image; the index of the largest value (7 for the first test digit, with probability 0.99999106) is the predicted class.
Predictions are made on test images, i.e. data the model never saw during training.

questions.question: After Listing 2.4, what are the shape and dtype of `train_images`?
questions.explanation: The page says the array is transformed from (60000, 28, 28) uint8 into a float32 array of shape (60000, 28 * 28) = (60000, 784). The samples axis stays first; the cast to float32 precedes the division by 255.

questions.question: Why is `astype("float32")` applied before `/ 255`, and what range do the values end up in?
questions.answer: So that the division is floating-point rather than integer arithmetic; the values end up in [0, 1].
questions.explanation: The book states the goal: 'scaling it so that all values are in the [0, 1] interval' and converting to a float32 array. Dividing a uint8 array directly would not produce the intended float32 fractions.

questions.question: With 60,000 training images, `batch_size=128` and `epochs=5`, how many weight updates does `fit()` perform?
questions.answer: ceil(60000/128) = 469 updates per epoch, times 5 epochs = 2,345 updates.
questions.explanation: Each batch yields one gradient update; 60000/128 = 468.75 so the last batch is partial and there are 469 per epoch. Section 2.5 (p.76) states these exact numbers.

questions.question: In Listing 2.6, what does `predictions[0]` contain?
options: The predicted digit for the first test image
Ten probabilities, one per digit class, for the first test image
The 784 pixel values of the first test image
The accuracy of the model on the first ten test images
questions.answer: Ten probabilities, one per digit class, for the first test image
questions.explanation: The page says each number of index i corresponds to the probability that `test_digits[0]` belongs to class i. The predicted digit requires an argmax (p.45); the pixels are in `test_digits[0]`; accuracy comes from `evaluate()` on p.45.

questions.question: The model reaches 0.989 accuracy during `fit()`. Why should you not conclude it will classify 98.9 % of new digits correctly?
questions.answer: Because that accuracy is measured on the training data the model learned from; performance on never-before-seen data is usually lower (97.8 % on the test set, p.45), a gap called overfitting.
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says the two displayed quantities are 'over the training data'. The next page compares with test accuracy and names the gap overfitting.

questions.question: What do the two keyword arguments `epochs=5` and `batch_size=128` in Listing 2.5 control?
questions.answer: `epochs=5`: the model passes over the entire training set five times; `batch_size=128`: the weights are updated after every group of 128 samples.
questions.explanation: This is the meaning given on p.76 ('iterate on the training data in mini-batches of 128 samples, 5 times over'); the page itself introduces the call as fitting the model to its training data.

questions.question: Could you write Listings 2.4 to 2.6 from memory and explain the purpose of each line to a classmate? Can you say why the test images must be preprocessed identically to the training images?
questions.answer: Reshape to (n, 784), cast to float32 and divide by 255 for both sets; fit for 5 epochs with batches of 128; slice ten test digits, predict, read the argmax. The test images must match the training preprocessing because the model's weights were learned for flat [0, 1] inputs.
